Catalytic Enantioselective Friedel–Crafts Allenylation
Priyotosh Das, Debangshu Ghosh, and Santanu Mukherjee*
Abstract: The first enantioselective Friedel-Crafts (FC)
allenylation reaction for the creation of central chirality
is developed under cooperative Ir(I)/(phosphoramidi-
te,olefin) and Lewis acid catalysis. This enantioconver-
gent reaction utilizes racemic allenylic alcohol as the
electrophile and shows compatibility with a variety of
electron-rich arenes and heteroarenes. The resulting
highly enantioenriched (up to > 99.5 : 0.5 e.r.) 1,1-disub-
stituted allenylic methanes, bearing a benzylic carbon
stereocenter, are obtained with complete regiocontrol –
both on (hetero)arenes as well as on the allenylic
fragment. This protocol allows for the enantioselective
formal introduction of a 4-carbon alkyl chain into
(hetero)arenes, along with the creation of a benzylic
stereocenter. Judicious synthetic elaborations not only
lead to formal enantioselective FC alkylation products
of less electron-rich arenes but also of substituted arenes
in ortho- and even meta-selective fashion. An intra-
molecular version of this FC allenylation is shown to
proceed with promising enantioselectivity under the
same catalytic conditions. Mechanistic studies revealed
the involvement of dynamic kinetic asymmetric trans-
formation (DyKAT) of racemic allenylic alcohols in this
reaction.
Introduction
Enantioselective introduction of an unfunctionalized alkyl
group into (hetero)arenes holds significant importance
owing to the prevalence of benzylic carbon stereocenters in
natural products and medicinally active compounds.
[1]
Notwithstanding the magnificent insurgence of transition
metal-catalyzed C � H activation chemistry during the past
decade,
[2]
Friedel–Crafts (FC) alkylation
[3]
remained argu-
ably the most straightforward strategy for the introduction
of unfunctionalized alkyl groups into (hetero)arenes
(Scheme 1A).
[4]
Over the years, a plethora of catalytic methods have
been instituted to achieve enantioselective FC reactions.
[5]
An overwhelming majority of these reactions relied on using
substrates bearing electrophilic sp
2
carbon center.
[5]
In
addition to being prochiral, functional groups present in
these substrates ease their activation and enantiofacial
discrimination (Scheme 1B). In contrast, the application of
electrophiles containing a reactive sp
3
carbon center in
enantioselective FC reactions has been scarce.
[6]
Such
racemic electrophilic substrates necessitate the intervention
of either a dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) or a dynamic
kinetic asymmetric transformation (DyKAT) pathway to
avoid using an overstoichiometric amount of electrophile.
[7]
For reactions proceeding via a prochiral intermediate (e.g.,
carbocation), discrimination between the two enantiotopic
faces becomes an enormous challenge due to the absence of
any functional group (Scheme 1B).
[8]
Transition metal-catalyzed allylic
[9–11]
and allenylic
substitutions
[11a]
are transformations that use electrophiles
bearing sp
3
carbon at the reaction center. Several inter- and
intramolecular enantioselective FC allylation reactions have
been developed under Pd
[12]
and Ir-catalysis
[13]
. However, the
closely related FC allenylation reaction, which would
formally introduce an unfunctionalized 4-carbon alkyl chain
into (hetero)arenes, with the generation of a benzylic carbon
stereocenter, remained largely unexplored (Scheme 1B)
During this study, a report by Yu, Shao, and co-workers
described a Pd-catalyzed FC allenylation of indoles for the
enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral allenes.
[14]
How-
ever, enantioselective FC allenylation for creating central
chirality remains an uncharted territory.
Iridium-catalyzed enantioselective allenylic substitution
reaction, introduced by Carreira et al. in 2018,
[15]
is mecha-
nistically distinct from its more widely explored palladium-
catalyzed variants.
[16,17]
Unlike the involvement of η
3
-Pd(II)-
butadienyl intermediates in Pd(0)-catalyzed allenylic
substitution,
[16,17]
the reactions catalyzed by Ir(I)/(phosphor-
amidite,olefin)-complex
[11c]
is proposed to proceed through a
carbocationic η
2
-Ir(I) intermediate A (Scheme 1C),
[15]
which
makes it a potential candidate for FC reaction. However,
(hetero)arenes are a class of nucleophiles which has never
been employed in this reaction. As such, only a few
nucleophiles have so far been explored in this Ir-catalyzed
enantioselective allenylic substitution reaction, namely al-
kylzinc reagents,
[15]
ammonia surrogates,
[18]
hydride (from
Hantzsch ester),
[19]
silyl ketene acetals
[20]
and vinyl azides
[21]
(Scheme 1C).
As a part of our ongoing research program dedicated to
the development of enantioselective C(sp
2
) � H allylation
[22]
and allenylation reactions, we decided to employ
(hetero)arenes as the nucleophile in Ir-catalyzed allenylation
reaction. However, (hetero)arenes are less reactive com-
pared to the previously utilized nucleophiles in this reaction
(see above).
[15,18–21]
Nonetheless, we reasoned that the
proposed η
2
-Ir(I)-bound allenylic carbocation would be
sufficiently electrophilic to be intercepted by suitably

substituted electron-rich (hetero)arenes and should facilitate
the desired FC reaction. Moreover, the proposed trigonal
bipyramidal coordination sphere of Ir(I) bearing two
(P,olefin) ligands, even though distant from the reaction
site, has been shown to offer necessary face-selectivity for
nucleophilic addition to the prochiral carbocation in A
(Scheme 1C).
[15,19]
Therefore, the same selectivity can be
expected in the enantiodetermining C � C bond formation
step with (hetero)arenes.
Apart from enantioselectivity, we were cognizant of two
regiochemical issues: While the regioselectivity on the
suggested allenylic carbocation A has been shown to be
reliably dictated in favor of nucleophilic addition at C4 (vs
C2) by the ligands on Ir (Scheme 1C),
[15]
the site selectivity
on the (hetero)arenes must be left to their innate reactivity.
Herein, we present the results of this investigation, which
culminated in the first Ir-catalyzed enantioselective Friedel–
Crafts allenylation (Scheme 1C).
Results and Discussion
At the outset of our study, FC allenylation of 3,5-dimeth-
oxyphenol 1 a with racemic allenylic alcohol rac-2 a in the
presence of 6 mol % of a catalyst derived from [Ir(COD)Cl]
2
and Carreira’s (P,olefin) ligand (S
a
)-L
[11c]
was selected as the
model reaction (Table 1).
The reason behind the choice of this substrate was
twofold. While the electron-rich nature of 1 a was reasoned
to facilitate the FC reaction, we were apprehensive of the
possible overalkylation processes. Therefore, it was essential
to identify reaction conditions that would favor only the
monoalkylated product. At the same time, we wanted to
verify the regioselectivity of the monoalkylation process
(i.e., ortho- vs para-substitution) with an unsymmetrical
arene such as 1 a.

The reaction with an excess of arene 1 a in THF at 50 ° C
using Sc(OTf)
3
as the Lewis acidic promoter indeed
furnished the FC allenylation product 3 aa (Table 1, entry 1).
Despite the low yield and modest enantioselectivity, the
formation of only the monoallenylation product with
complete regioselectivity in favor of ortho- was encouraging
and provided the impetus for further investigation. In line
with earlier studies,
[15,18–21]
no diene product, arising from the
addition of 1 a at C2 of A (Scheme 1C), could be detected.
Screening of other Lewis and Brønsted acidic promoters
(entries 2–8) revealed Fe(OTf)
2
and La(OTf)
3
to be nearly
equally efficient as 3 aa was isolated with similar levels of
yield and enantiomeric ratio (e.r.) in both these cases
(entries 3 and 6). Notably, a stronger Lewis acid Bi(OTf)
3
led to the complete decomposition of 2 a, and no 3 aa could
be detected (entry 2). At this stage, we decided to use
Fe(OTf)
2
for further optimization. The reaction in toluene
was found to be faster, but 3 aa was formed with diminished
e.r. (entry 10). In this reaction, no allenylation product of
toluene could be detected despite its presence in large
excess, which underscores the importance of electron-rich
substituents on the arene ring in rendering it nucleophilic
(see below). It is possible to carry out this reaction at room
temperature without much influence on the enantioselectiv-
ity (entry 11). Although expectedly slower, the reaction at
room temperature makes the process operationally simpler.
Combining the effect of toluene in improving the reaction
rate and that of THF in enhancing the enantioselectivity led
to the identification of a 1 : 1 mixture of THF and toluene as
the optimum reaction medium when 3 aa was isolated in
71 % yield with 98 : 2 e.r. (entry 12). Under the same reaction
conditions, La(OTf)
3
delivered 3 aa with a much inferior
yield and enantioselectivity (entry 13). Efforts to ameliorate
the reaction outcome by tweaking other reaction parameters
proved unsuccessful.
[23]
The catalyst, promoter, and the reaction conditions
optimized for the FC allenylation of 3,5-dimethoxyphenol
1 a (Table 1, entry 12) were then extended to other arenes
and heteroarenes for reaction with racemic allenylic alcohol
rac-2 a (Scheme 2). We were delighted that our protocol is
not restricted to electron-rich phenols such as 1 a. Structur-
ally and electronically related arenes such as 1,3,5-trimeth-
oxybenzene 1 b and 3-methoxy-N,N-dimethylaniline 1 c
fared equally well under our reaction conditions and
afforded allenylic arenes 3 ba and 3 ca, respectively, with
similar level of yields and enantioselectivities (Scheme 2A).
With 1 c as the substrate, allenylation took place exclusively
at para- to dimethylamino group. The presence of hydroxy
or methoxy group on the arene ring is not a prerequisite for
this reaction. Replacing the methoxy group in 1 c with a less
electron-releasing methyl doesn’t appear to affect the
reactivity of 1 d, as the regioselective para-product 3 da was
isolated in 84 % yield and with 99 : 1 e.r. In fact, FC
allenylation of N,N-dimethylaniline (1 e) and other analo-
gous N,N-dialkylaniline derivatives (1 f–i) themselves were
found to occur efficiently and selectively at the para-position
of the N,N-dialkylamine substituent in moderate to good
yield with good to excellent enantioselectivity. Naphthalene
derivatives (1 j–l), adorned with electron-rich substituents,
are viable substrates for this allenylic arylation reaction.
However, these reactions turned out to be much less
efficient and enantioselective. Unfortunately, electronically
lesser endowed arenes such as phenol, anisole, and naphthol
(both α- and β-) failed to react under our optimized
conditions.
[23]
In the realm of heteroarenes, indole (1 m) as well as N-
substituted indoles (1 n–o) served as excellent substrates and
furnished 3-allenylic indoles 3 ma–oa in very high yield with
superb enantioselectivity (Scheme 2B). The reaction with 2-
methylindole (1 p), although somewhat sluggish, was equally
enantioselective. In the case of 3-methylindole (1 q), 2-
allenylic indole 3 qa was formed in 73 % yield with 98 : 2 e.r.
Whether this reaction proceeds by direct 2-allenylation or
via initial 3-allenylation of indole followed by stereospecific
rearrangement could not be confirmed at this stage. Pyrrole
(1 r) and its derivatives (1 s–u) showed fairly good reactiv-
ities, even though enantioselectivities varied depending on
the nature and the position of the substituents. While
pyrrole (1 r) itself and N-phenylpyrrole (1 s) afforded the 2-
allenylation products 3 ra and 3 sa, respectively, with ex-
cellent enantioselectivities, the reactions of 2-methylpyrrole
(1 t) and particularly 2,4-dimethylpyrrole (1 u) took place
with significantly reduced enantioselectivity. 3-Meth-
oxythiophene (1 v), on the other hand, turned out to be a
suitable substrate and delivered 2-allenylic thiophene deriv-
ative 3 va selectively with an outstanding e.r. of > 99.5 : 0.5.
Among other heteroarenes tested, (benzo)furans, carba-
zoles, and N-methylimidazole were found to be unsuitable
substrates for FC allenylation under our optimized protocol,
presumably due to their reduced nucleophilicity.
[23]
For showcasing the scope of allenylic alcohols, 1,3,5-
trimethoxybenzene (1 b) was chosen as the nucleophile. The
examples compiled in Scheme 3A indicate the generality of
this enantioselective FC allenylation protocol with respect to
racemic allenylic alcohols bearing aryl substituents. Elec-
tronically diverse substituents on various positions of the
aryl ring were well tolerated and furnished the desired
products generally in high yield and with excellent enantio-
selectivity. Of specific note is the FC product 3 bk, which
bears a boronate functionality and could be subjected to
diversification through various cross-coupling reactions. The
enantiopurity of 1-bromonaphthyl-substituted product 3 bp
could be further improved after a single crystallization.
Single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis of crystals thus
obtained for 3 bp established its absolute configuration to be
(S) (CCDC 2302758, Scheme 3A).
[24]
Configuration of the
other FC allenylation products shown in this report were
assigned in analogy with 3 bp.
Apart from aryl substituents, as shown in Scheme 3A,
allenylic alcohols containing heterocyclic substituents, such
as 1,3-benzodioxole, indole, furan, and thiophene, could also
be utilized as allenylic electrophile for reaction with 1 b
(Scheme 3B)
However, most of these reactions were relatively less
enantioselective than their aryl counterparts. While most
aliphatic allenylic alcohols failed to react under our
optimized conditions,
[23]
cyclopropyl-substituted allenylic
alcohol 2 v displayed substantial reactivity and furnished the

could be detected when tertiary allenylic alcohol was used as
the electrophilic partner for reaction with 1 b, even at
50 ° C.
[23]
In the Ir-catalyzed enantioselective allenylic substitution
reactions reported to date, allenylic alcohols or their
derivatives, bearing monosubstituted allene unit, have most
commonly been employed as the allenylic electrophile.
Reactions with allenylic alcohols, having disubstituted allene
unit, have been shown to be less efficient and considerably
less enantioselective.
[15,18]
We were pleased to find 2,2-
disubstituted allenylic alcohol 2 w to be a competent
substrate for our FC allenylation reaction. However, as
expected, 2 w was found to be less reactive compared to its
monosubstituted analogue 2 a. Accordingly, the reaction
needed to be carried out at an elevated temperature (50 ° C),
and the product 3 bw was obtained with moderate e.r.
Having showcased the broad generality of both the
reaction partners in this enantioselective FC allenylation
reaction, we recognized the potential of our protocol in
providing access to both the product enantiomers under the
influence of a single catalyst antipode – simply through the
choice of substrates. The implementation of this strategy
was demonstrated by enantiodivergent synthesis of diary-
lallenylic methane 3 es (Scheme 4). The reaction of N,N-
dimethylaniline 1 e with N-tosyl-3-indolyl substituted alle-

one of the indole moieties. Similarly, the reaction of indole
(1 m) with N-tosyl-2-indolyl substituted allenylic alcohol
(2 y) furnished another bis(indolyl)allenylic methane 3 my

two indole rings (C2 and C3) with the stereocenter.
Enantioselective synthesis of both 3 ms and 4 could be

As shown in Scheme 2, indoles (1 m–o) and indoline (1 i)
display different regioselectivity in this FC reaction. This
innate reactivity pattern of indole and its derivatives was
exploited for the regiodivergent allenylation of indoles
(Scheme 6). While direct FC reaction of N-methylindole
(1 n) led to 3-allenylic indole 3 na, a two-step protocol
consisting of FC allenylation of N-methylindoline (1 i)
[25]
followed by oxidation with MnO
2
[13b]
resulted in 5-allenylic
indole 5 in 47 % overall yield with 98 : 2 e.r. Similarly,
starting from 4,7-dihydro-1H-indole (1 w), FC allenylation
and oxidative aromatization with p-benzoquinone
[26]
fur-
nished 2-allenylic indole 6. Unfortunately, 6 was found to be
sensitive to silica gel and configurationally labile.
Apart from the 1.0 mmol scale reactions depicted for
3 ba and 3 ca in Scheme 2, this enantioselective FC allenyla-
tion reaction can be further scaled up with lower catalyst
loading. As exemplified for the reaction between 1 a and
rac-2 a in the presence of 4 mol % in situ generated Ir[(S
a
)-
L]
2
Cl, both the catalytic activity as well as the yield and
enantioselectivity were retained even with a 20-fold increase
in the scale of the reaction (Scheme 7A).
The allene moiety in allenylic arenes can act as a
linchpin for synthetic elaboration to other building blocks,
especially in cooperation with functionalities at the ortho-
position of the arene ring. Molybdenum-catalyzed hydro-
silylation of allene in 3 ba proved to be highly regio- and
diastereoselective and resulted in (Z)-allylsilane 7 in 61 %
yield (Scheme 7B).
[27]
Rhodium-catalyzed intramolecular
hydroalkoxylation of 3 aa gave dihydrobenzofuran derivative
8 exclusively as the cis-isomer in 84 % yield.
[28]
The
corresponding trans-dihydrobenzofuran 9 can be obtained
under gold-catalysis,
[29]
but with considerably less d.r.
Organocatalytic intramolecular iodoetherification
[30]
of 3 aa
worked reasonably well under bifunctional tertiary amino-
thiourea epi-QD-TU to give 2-iodovinyl dihydrobenzofuran
derivative 10, albeit with only 2.2 : 1 d.r.
Hydrogenation of the allene functionality allows for the
formal introduction of an unfunctionalized 4-carbon alkyl
chain into a (hetero)arene ring with the creation of a
benzylic carbon stereocenter as shown for the conversion of
3 aa to 11 (Scheme 7B). The presence of the hydroxy group
in 11 provides a handle for installing other functional groups
on the arene ring through the intermediacy of the corre-
sponding triflate 12. For instance, Pd-catalyzed Suzuki
coupling of 12 with phenylboronic acid gave biaryl deriva-
tive 13 in excellent yield. Another Pd-catalyzed coupling
with diphenylphosphine oxide led to 14 through the
formation of a C–P bond. The triflate group in 12 can also
be removed under Pd-catalyzed hydrogenolytic conditions
using triethylammonium formate
[31]
to furnish the formal FC
alkylation product of 1,3-dimethoxybenzene 15 – directly
inaccessible via FC allenylation reaction due to insufficient
nucleophilicity of 1,3-dimethoxybenzene.
The use of N,N-dialkylaniline derivatives as a nucleo-
phile in the FC allenylation reaction is equally advantageous
for accessing formal FC alkylation products of less electron-
rich arenes. Cleavage of the dialkylamino substituents from
arenes is possible following the two-step protocol developed
by MacMillan et al.
[32]
Thus, allenylic arenes 3 ca and 3 da
could be transformed into formal FC alkylation products of
anisole (17) and toluene (19), respectively, in excellent yield
(Scheme 7C, eq 1). This synthetic maneuver not only
allowed for the access of FC alkylation products of
inherently inert nucleophiles, such as toluene and anisole, in
the Ir-catalyzed FC allenylation reaction (see above) but
also ensures the otherwise challenging ‘ortho-selectivity’ in
the products 17 and 19.
The exposure of 6-allenylic N-methyl tetrahydroquino-
line 3 ha to this three-step protocol resulted in the rupture of
the tetrahydroquinoline ring to form 21 (Scheme 7C, eq 2).
This strategy presents a facile and enantioselective route to
‘meta-selective’ formal FC alkylation products through the
utilization of cyclic N,N-dialkylaniline derivatives as the
nucleophile. Starting from the tricyclic substrate 3 ga, the
same synthetic manipulation led to meta,meta-disubstituted
formal FC alkylation product 23, with the concomitant
formation of a 10-membered macrocycle (Scheme 7C, eq 3).
Despite notable progress in asymmetric allenylic sub-
stitution reactions under Pd and Ir-catalysis, there has been
no report on their intramolecular variants.
[33]
After exploring
the scope and limitations of this Ir-catalyzed enantioselec-
tive FC allenylation reaction, we wondered about the
viability of the same catalyst system for an intramolecular

To
understand the nature of the reactive intermediate in this
FC reaction, an intermolecular competition experiment was
conducted using an equimolar mixture of an electron-rich
and an electron-poor allenylic alcohol 2 e and 2 h, respec-
tively (Scheme 9C). With 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (1 b) as
the nucleophile under our standard catalytic conditions, 2 e
was found to react faster than 2 h. The higher reactivity of
2 e can be ascribed to the greater stabilization of the
intermediate and the subsequent transition state having
carbocationic character.
The ionization step (i.e., the conversion of 27 and 28,
respectively, to 29 and 30) is expected to be stereospecific
and hence sow the seed for a potential kinetic resolution
(KR) of allenylic alcohol. However, the use of allenylic
alcohols as the limiting reagent in our enantioselective FC
reaction and isolation of products with excellent e.r. in
> 50 % yield contradict this possibility. Moreover, the
reaction between 1 a and rac-2 a under our standard catalytic
conditions, when stopped ahead of time (40 min), led to the
recovery of unreacted 2 a as a racemic mixture (Scheme 9D,
entry 1). This experiment ruled out the intervention of a KR
in this reaction. Similar experiments with enantioenriched
2 a did not show any racemization of 2 a during the FC
reaction (Scheme 9D, entries 2–3), indicating that dynamic
kinetic resolution (DKR) is not operative either.
When using (S
a
)-L, the bottom faces of the planar
cationic butadienylium fragment in anti-29 and syn-30 are
hindered by the axially bound binaphthyl moiety on Ir(I)
(Scheme 9A).
[15]
Therefore, nucleophilic attack of 1 a from
the exposed top face (i.e., re- in anti-29 and si- in syn-30)
should result in (R)- and (S)-3 aa, respectively. Between
these two intermediates, syn-30 is more congested compared
to anti-29, due to the vicinity of phenyl ring to the sterically
hindered Ir-center. Therefore, the reaction is channeled
through anti-29, to furnish (R)-3 aa as the major product.
Starting from enantioenriched 2 a, when the FC reaction was
carried out using racemic (P,olefin) ligand rac-L, the
product 3 aa was formed as a racemic mixture (Scheme 9D,
entry 4). Evidently, the stereochemical information present
in allenylic alcohol is lost during the reaction, and the
product configuration is exclusively dictated by the ligand
on iridium. The loss of stereochemical information of the
starting allenylic alcohol 2 a can be explained by the facile
equilibration between the Ir-bound carbocationic intermedi-
ates 29 and 30 through rotation around the C3 � C4 bond.
The overall reaction represents a dynamic kinetic asymmet-
ric transformation (DyKAT) of the racemic allenylic alco-
hols.
C onclusions
In conclusion, (hetero)arenes were employed for the first
time as nucleophiles in Ir-catalyzed allenylic substitution
reaction and led to the development of the first catalytic
enantioselective Friedel-Crafts allenylation for creating
central chirality.
[34]
Using easily accessible racemic allenylic
alcohols as the electrophile, this reaction is catalyzed by a
cooperative combination of a Ir(I)-
bis(phosphoramidite,olefin) complex and Lewis acidic Fe-

Hydrogenation of the allene functionality in the products

Preliminary experiments established the feasibility of an
enantioselective intramolecular FC allenylation using ter-
tiary allenylic alcohols as substrate under the same catalytic
conditions. The latter finding is particularly exciting as it
leads to the enantioselective construction of a diaryl-
containing all-carbon-quaternary center. Experiments to-
wards mechanistic elucidation revealed dynamic kinetic
asymmetric transformation (DyKAT) of racemic allenylic
alcohols as the reason for enantioconvergency in this FC
allenylation reaction.
